title: The five stages of making a film
description: A film moves through development, pre-production, production (the shoot) and post-production, then distribution brings it to audiences.

facts.text: Britannica describes the film value chain as running from the selection of an idea that could become a film to the film's consumption in a movie theater or on television.

Film production is usually composed of four phases: development, preproduction, filming and postproduction; the finished master copy is then sold to a distributor, which makes copies for theatrical release.

In development, a producer picks an original idea or buys the rights to an existing story, such as a novel, a comic book, a play or a game, has a writer develop a screenplay, estimates the costs and looks for money.
Preproduction work includes developing the script, auditioning the actors and planning how each scene will be shot.
The shooting phase usually lasts a few weeks and is delicate and expensive, because it involves the simultaneous work of several people.

title: Post-production turns footage into a finished film
description: Post-production usually lasts longer than the shoot: picture and sound are edited, effects, titles, music and sound effects are added, and everything is combined.

facts.text: The postproduction stage is likely to last longer than the shooting itself; picture and sound are edited, effects and titles are created, music and sound effects are added, and all are combined.

title: How a screenplay is laid out
description: A screenplay is the written basis of a film; each scene opens with a capitalized scene heading (INT. or EXT., place, time of day), followed by action lines and dialogue under capitalized character names.

facts.text: Britannica defines a screenplay as the written text that provides the basis for a film production.
In the Academy Nicholl Fellowships format guide, a scene heading, or slug line, is always in capitals and usually begins with INT. or EXT.; character names above dialogue are also in capitals.

A scene heading tells whether the scene is inside or outside, where it takes place and the time of day; action lines describe what the audience will see, and each speaker's name is in capitals with the dialogue below.

title: One screenplay page is about one minute
description: Because screenplays share one standard format (Courier, fixed margins), one page works out to about a minute of screen time, a rule of thumb used to estimate running time, budgets and schedules.

facts.text: Syd Field wrote that one page of screenplay is approximately one minute of screen time, whether the script is all action, all dialogue or a mix, and called it a good rule of thumb.
The Academy Nicholl Fellowships format guide calls Courier, 12-point, 10-pitch, the industry standard font for screenplays and advises against other fonts.

The page-per-minute estimate grew from the typewriter-era standard format: Courier, whose characters each take the same space, with standardized margins and spacing; studios use it to estimate budgets and shooting schedules.
One page per minute is only an estimate: a short action description can play for minutes on screen, while rapid-fire dialogue often runs faster than a minute a page.

title: Storyboards: the film drawn shot by shot
description: A storyboard is a shot-by-shot visual plan of a film, one panel per camera shot; the Disney studio pioneered it, and simple sketches are enough.

facts.text: ACMI, a museum of screen culture in Melbourne, describes a storyboard as a shot-by-shot visual plan that shows what a film will look like before it is shot; each panel represents a camera shot, and it guides the team shooting the film.
A storyboard does not recreate every frame of a film and need not be a work of art: simple sketches with stick figures can show the shot type and what is in the shot.
The Walt Disney Family Museum says the Walt Disney Studios pioneered storyboarding.
A storyboard is a series of sketches that maps out a story, letting filmmakers see the plot in sequence, judge whether the story is clear and spot plot holes or inconsistencies.

title: The shot list: every shot to capture
description: A shot list keeps track of every planned shot and its details, such as camera movement, so the crew knows what to film on the day.

facts.text: A shot list keeps track of all the shots so that, when filming comes, the crew knows what it needs to film; on set, filmmakers often keep the storyboard and script on hand to set up shots as planned.
A shot list can list each shot's camera movement; 'static' in that column means the camera should not move.

title: Producer and director
description: The producer manages a film's money and schedule from financing to final approval; the director develops the artistic vision and oversees each scene.

facts.text: Producers are a film's managers, from securing the financing in preproduction to approving the completed film; they hire the director, create the budget and approve changes to the script, budget or schedule.
The director develops and implements the film's artistic vision: helping choose the cast, overseeing the shooting of each scene, working closely with the cinematographer and guiding the actors.

title: Cinematographer, gaffer and grip
description: The cinematographer (director of photography) shoots the scenes and decides camera moves, lenses and lighting; the gaffer designs the lighting scheme; grips carry out the lighting plan and support the camera.

facts.text: The cinematographer, also called the director of photography, is in charge of shooting the scenes and decides how the camera should move to meet the director's vision.
A cinematographer chooses the camera and lenses to use and how to light each scene, and works closely with the director on setting up shots.

Gaffers supervise the electricians on a film set and design and adjust the lighting scheme for each scene; if a scene needs a campfire that can't be built on set, gaffers use lights to recreate its flicker.
The AFI's glossary defines the gaffer as the chief electrician on a film or television set.
Grips carry out the gaffer's lighting plan and may support the camera operator when the camera is rigged on a dolly or crane; the key grip oversees the other grips.

title: The script supervisor keeps continuity
description: The script supervisor records what was shot and how, take by take, so the footage cuts together seamlessly.

facts.text: A script supervisor records slate numbers, notes on each take, lenses, the action and running times, plus details of props, makeup and costume, so that the footage shot will cut together seamlessly.
The BFI describes film continuity as something that, by its nature, should be entirely invisible.

title: Shot sizes: wide, medium and close-up
description: Shots are named by how close the camera is to the subject: a wide (long) shot shows the whole body and setting, a medium shot roughly the waist up, a close-up the head.

facts.text: A shot type is defined by how close the camera is to the subject being filmed, which is usually a character but can be a setting or an object.
In a wide shot or long shot you see a character's whole body from head to toe, sometimes small within the landscape or space around them.
A medium shot, or mid shot, generally shows a character from roughly the waist up and is good for showing body language and a character performing actions.
In a close-up a person's head fills the frame; close-ups are good for showing emotion on characters' faces.
Shot scales are not universal: whether a shot counts as a close-up is judged in relation to the other shots in the same film.

title: What each shot size is for
description: Wide shots establish where a scene is and keep full-body action in view; close-ups draw viewers into a character's emotion.

facts.text: Establishing shots show the audience where a scene takes place and are usually long shots; extreme long shots are usually the first or last shots of a sequence.
Because a long shot can show a whole body moving without reframing, it is common in genres where full-body action must be seen, such as Hollywood musicals and 1970s martial arts films.
If a director wants the audience more emotionally involved in a key scene, the cinematographer might shoot the actors' faces at close range to capture their expressions.
A close-up can capture subtle emotion, such as a character trying hard to hide their feelings, not only extreme emotions like crying or fear.

title: Camera angles: eye level, low and high
description: Most shots are at eye level; a low angle looks up and can make a character seem strong or menacing, a high angle looks down and can make them seem small or weak.

facts.text: Eye level is the most standard camera angle; a large share of shots are taken from eye level because it is easy and natural for viewers.
In a low-angle shot the camera is placed well below eye level, facing up; it can make a character look heroic and strong, or a villain scary and intimidating.
In a high-angle shot the camera is above the character, angled down; it can make characters look small and weak.

In The Color of Paradise (1999), Majid Majidi's Iranian film, the father who rules his family is often shot from a low angle, and his blind son Mohammad and elderly grandmother from a high angle, stressing their dependence and smallness.
Readings of camera angles are not fixed: in The Color of Paradise, the high-angle view of Mohammad and his grandmother may also suggest that God is watching over them.

title: The Dutch (canted) angle
description: Tilting the camera so the frame is not level creates a sense of chaos, instability or unease.

facts.text: In a canted framing, also called a Dutch angle, the frame is not level; it creates an impression of chaos and instability and is often used when a character experiences something unusual or distressing.

title: Pans and tilts: turning the camera in place
description: Camera movement changes framing during a shot; a pan turns the camera horizontally and a tilt swivels it up or down while it stays in one spot.

facts.text: Britannica describes camera movement as moving the camera during shooting to alter framing, scale and shooting angle.
A pan turns the camera horizontally, left or right, sweeping around the scene; the word comes from panorama. A pan can follow someone or reveal something.
A tilt moves the camera from angled down to angled up, or the reverse; tilts are often used to show the scale of a building, starting at its base.

title: Dolly, crane and handheld shots
description: In tracking shots the camera itself travels, often on a dolly; cranes lift it through the air; handheld shooting uses the operator's body; a zoom only enlarges part of the image.

facts.text: In a tracking shot the framing travels through space forward, backward or sideways; the camera often rides a dolly, a small wheeled platform that runs on track or is moved by hand.
A heavy dolly holding the camera and a seated operator can be pushed or driven around the set; if the ground is not smooth, rails like train tracks are laid for it.
In a crane shot the camera, on a crane (a large cantilevered arm), moves through the air above the ground; crane shots can give the viewer a feeling of omniscience over the characters.

When the camera dollies, distances change, so the spatial relationship between objects in the frame changes; a zoom changes only the focal length, enlarging part of the frame without changing perspective, which gives it a flat look.

Handheld shooting uses the camera operator's body as the support; newsreel and wartime operators favored small cameras, later taken up by documentary makers; it is cheap and feels spontaneous but jerky, and gyroscopic Steadicams from the 1970s made smooth moving shots possible.

title: Focal length: wide-angle, normal and telephoto
description: A normal lens (50 mm on 35 mm film) looks like the eye's view; wide-angle lenses take in more and exaggerate depth, telephoto lenses compress it, though perspective really comes from camera distance.

facts.text: A normal lens reproduces perspective similar to the human eye; for 35 mm film a normal lens is 50 mm; shorter lenses are wide-angle and lenses two or more times longer are telephoto.
A wide-angle lens has a short focal length and lets more space into the frame, which makes it handy for shooting in a real room; it exaggerates the distance between foreground and background.
A wide-angle lens exaggerates depth and a telephoto compresses it: a person walking toward the camera seems to approach faster with a wide-angle and slower with a telephoto.

Picture perspective depends on the camera-to-subject distance, not on the lens: from the same distance, different lenses change the area of view but not the perspective, and a telephoto shot is almost always taken from farther away.

title: Depth of field and focus
description: Depth of field is how much of the image, near to far, is sharp; shallow focus isolates one plane to direct attention, and a rack focus shifts focus during a shot.

facts.text: Depth of field is the distance through which elements in an image are in sharp focus; bright light, a narrow aperture and a wide-angle lens tend to give more of it.
Shallow focus keeps only one plane sharp; it directs the viewer's attention to one element without a cut and is very common in close-ups.
Racking focus changes the lens's focus during a shot so one plane goes out of focus as another comes in, steering the viewer's attention and linking two spaces or objects.

title: Three-point lighting
description: The standard lighting of classical narrative film uses a key light, a fill light that softens its shadows, and a backlight that separates the subject from the background.

facts.text: Britannica says lighting helps set the tone and emphasize specific parts of a scene.

Three-point lighting is the standard scheme of classical narrative cinema, and most mainstream films rely on it: a bright key light highlights the subject, a fill light from the opposite side keeps the key's shadows faint, and a backlight picks the subject out from the background.
Documentaries and realist cinema often rely on natural light instead of three-point lighting, to create a sense of authenticity.

title: High-key and low-key lighting
description: High-key lighting raises the fill almost to the key for bright, shadowless images; low-key lighting uses little fill for strong contrast and deep shadows.

facts.text: High-key lighting raises the fill light almost to the level of the key light, producing bright images with few shadows; it is typical of entertainment genres such as musicals and comedies.
Low-key lighting uses very little fill light, creating strong contrast between bright and dark and shadows that obscure parts of the subjects; it is associated with suspense genres such as film noir.

title: The clapperboard marks each take
description: A clapperboard's slate identifies the take, and its snapping arm marks one instant on both picture and sound so editors can synchronize them.

facts.text: A clapper, or clapperboard, is a slate showing information about the take, topped by a hinged arm; its wooden jaws, about a foot long, are snapped together in the picture so the clack registers on both picture and sound.
When sound and picture are recorded separately, the clapper's shared visual and audio cue lets editors match the sound to the images.
